summary: For ages 7–9, help children see that a place's typical weather is not random but shaped by a few predictable geographic causes: distance from the Equator (latitude) is the main control on temperature, with altitude (higher is generally colder) and nearness to the sea (which usually evens out hot and cold extremes and can bring moisture) as major secondary factors. Children first establish the Equator-to-pole temperature gradient, then isolate one factor at a time, 'obtain and combine' information from at least two sources (map plus climate data or photos), and confront common confusions such as 'the South is always hot', 'higher means hotter', and 'all deserts are hot'.
misconceptions: Latitude is the only thing that matters — altitude and nearness to the sea also strongly shape local weather
'The South is always hot / the North is always cold' — ignores hemispheres and that both poles are cold
Mountains near the Equator must be hot — high altitude makes them cold despite low latitude
Deserts are always hot — some (e.g. polar/high deserts) are cold; 'desert' means dry, not hot
Weather in a place is random rather than shaped by predictable geographic factors

activities.title: Climate map: vary one cause at a time
steps: Drop a place-marker somewhere on a world map and read its typical weather (e.g. typical temperature and whether it is wet or dry).
Drag the marker from the poles toward the Equator and describe the overall trend in temperature along the way (watch for places, like high mountains, that break the pattern).

Park a place on the Equator at low altitude (hot all year), then raise its ALTITUDE and describe what happens to its weather; then move a place next to the sea and describe how its hot/cold extremes change.
Combine a map view with a climate data or photo card into a short spoken or written summary: 'This place is ___ because ___.'
activities.insight: A place's weather is the combined effect of a few geographic causes you can switch on and off: latitude sets the baseline, altitude cools, and the sea evens out extremes.

activities.title: Spinning globe: why the Equator is hotter
steps: Rotate a globe and locate the Equator and the North and South Poles.
Shine a movable sunlight beam onto the globe and compare how directly the rays strike near the Equator versus near the poles.
Explain in your own words why places near the Equator tend to be hotter, using the idea of direct versus glancing sunlight.
activities.insight: The Equator is hotter because sunlight hits it more directly, while it strikes the poles at a glancing angle — a spatial cause for the temperature gradient.

activities.title: Compare contrasting real places
steps: Study photo and climate-data cards for contrasting places: a tropical rainforest, a hot desert, a temperate coast, a polar region, and a high mountain.
Describe the typical weather of at least three of these climate types in your own words.
Sort or sequence the places from coldest to hottest and say which geographic factor best explains each place's weather.
Explain how a cold desert or a cold high desert can be a 'desert' — point out that 'desert' means dry, not hot.
activities.insight: Different places have very different typical weather, and for each case children can name a geographic factor (latitude, altitude, or nearness to the sea) that helps explain it, while knowing other things such as winds and mountains blocking rain also play a part.

activities.title: Same latitude, different weather (diagnostic discussion)
steps: Consider two towns at the same distance from the Equator on the same day and time of year: one high on a mountain, one by the sea. Explain why their weather might be quite different.
Answer: which single factor would you change to make the mountain town's weather more like the coastal town's?
Discuss: it snows on a mountain in a hot country near the Equator — how can that be?
Discuss: why do coastal places often have milder winters than inland places at the same latitude?
activities.insight: When latitude is held equal, you must appeal to other factors — altitude, nearness to the sea, wind — to explain a difference, and you can isolate which factor is doing the work.

activities.title: Voices from contrasting climates (enrichment)
steps: Read or listen to short accounts from people living in contrasting climates (e.g. tropical, desert, polar, mountain) describing their typical weather and daily life.
Match each account to its climate type and name the geographic factor that most shapes that place's weather.
activities.insight: Real human experiences can make distant climates vivid and relatable, and each can be tied back to the geographic causes behind that place's weather.

checkQuestion: Two towns are at the same distance from the equator on the same day and time of year. One sits high on a mountain, the other by the sea. Why might their weather be quite different?
checkAnswer: Factors besides latitude shape local weather: altitude (higher is colder), nearness to the sea (the ocean moderates temperature and adds moisture), and things like prevailing wind and mountains. So the same latitude can still mean very different local weather.
